review:
This game...it's damn near perfect. The art direction and animation are really tight and well executed, the controls are something to be envied and are incredibly well done, the music is captivating and remains in my head well after I've put the controller down...I am completely and utterly head over heels for this game. 

I look forward to exploring more in this game. The sense of accomplishment you feel from gaining a new ability to reach a part of the map that was previously unavailable is particularly satisfying. I wish I had more time for this amazing experience.

I can't recommend this game enough. Anyone considering this game, don't consider. Just buy. Install. Play. You won't be sorry.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] If you have even the slightest interest in either MetroidVania games, Platformers or anything cutesy: [b]This is a must buy for you![/b]
If neither of those apply to you, give it a try anyway, you might still fall in love with it as I did :)

[b]Pros and Cons:[/b]
+ Stunning visuals and great animation quality
+ Amazing soundtrack
+ Emotional story
+ Relatable characters, despite the fact that barely a word is spoken
+ The design, "voice" and animations of Ori will make even the most heartless bastard want to squeeze and cuddle her / him
+ Hard as balls, but fair (for the most part)
+ Some unique mechanics (for example guiding enemy projectiles while using them to change direction / boost your jump midair)

- When you beat the story, you can no longer go back to your save. 
So don't put the last bit of exploration off until after the last story bit, or you'll have to play through the entire game again for that one single secret and the 2% of map space you missed ><
(yes, I'm salty...)

[b]Story:[/b]
I usually talk a lot about the story in my reviews, but for this one, I kind of don't want to tell too much.
It's not a huge story and it's perhaps not quite as "perfect" as some people say it is, but it is very emotional and deserves to be experienced unspoiled.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
At its core, Ori is a MetroidVania game, but with a heavy emphasis on precision platforming.
The controls are tight and precise and traversing the environment feels really fun.
The difficulty is hard enough to really give you that sense of accomplishment that many gamers crave, without being frustrating.
It can get really intense at some points though.
You set your own checkpoints, which is interesting and helpful, but can be a bit disheartening when you die and realize that you forgot to set one for half an hour ^^"

You start off with just a jump and a basic attack, but as you go through the game you'll get a lot of different abilities, some of them very unique to the genre.
One for example allows you to bounce yourself off an enemy projectile, in any direction while sending it the opposite direction.
You also have an upgrade system where you can spend points to enhance your abilities and gain new ones.

There's a ton of secrets to find, like health and energy upgrades, or more points to upgrade.
They are often not easy to get to and there's a real satisfaction to finally reaching some of them.

Of course, there will be a lot of backtracking if you're planning to get all of them, as is typical for the genre.
But it doesn't really feel that way, since after gaining new abilities, the way you traverse the previously done sectors will have changed completely.

[b]Level Design:[/b]
The level design is close to perfection.
There's a real flow to traversing the environments if you do it well and there's a lot of secrets and hidden passages to discover.

The main path usually leaves some room for errors, so it won't be frustrating, while the secrets and shortcuts often require perfect timing and control to reach, giving the people that want it the ultimate difficulty, without putting up roadblocks for lesser skilled players.

Many of the secrets that require abilities that you'll learn later on are kept just slightly out of reach, giving you that desire to come back later when you can finally get them.

Despite how perfectly planned out all the sections are, it still feels very natural, like that's just how this world is, which does a lot to help the atmosphere.

[b]Soundtrack:[/b]
The soundtrack is a beautiful mix of orchestral music and choral vocals that carries a lot of emotion.
Whether calm, cheery, haunting or intense, it always fits the current situation perfectly.
It's rare for me to buy game soundtracks, but this one I bought and loaded onto my Mp3 player, so I can listen to it wherever I go.

[b]Visuals:[/b]
The aesthetic in this game is wonderful. Honestly, it's perhaps the most beautiful looking 2D game I've ever played in my entire life.
The environments are varied and interesting, the characters are adorable, the lighting is intense and colorful, the background paintings are stunning and the animations just make everything feel a lot more alive.

[b]Final Thoughts:[/b]
I played through this game in just 2 sittings and I can't wait to play through it again.
Even tough I usually dislike MetroidVania game and I'm not too fond of platformers, this has easily become one of my top 10 favorite games of all time.
Despite the fact that I usually don't give a damn about achievements, I want them all.
Despite the fact that I have no interest in Steam playing cards, I will collect them, because I want the badges and backgrounds.
If you didn't buy it because it didn't seem like your thing, give it a try anyway.
I think you won't regret it :)

Everyone should play this game.

I've never written a review of a Steam game, so take the existence of this one as a testament to the impact it had on me.

The gameplay is fantastic, sort of like Metroid, sort of like Donkey Kong, sort of like so many other classics. And yet Ori stands on its own. 
Ori is intuitive; it's inventive; it's surprisingly challenging (I died over 200 times in the 10 hours it took me to complete it.) But damn, is it fun. 
Everything is seamless. And I mean everything. From the minimalist interface, to the controls, to the microsecond load time between dying and respawning - the latter of which you, like me, will come to know well. And equally well the fact that you can save, more or less, wherever you want.
Power ups and ability trees keep things fresh, and like a good piece of Zelda equipment, every addition to your platforming repertoire opens up a whole new mechanic to the gameplay.

The story is as flawless as the game. (And the opening is as memorable as the ending. Have ready a bucket for your tears.)
Few action platformers have a decent story to accompany it. Ori is different. No, the game doesn’t play itself; it isn’t one of those. Rather, like a player to respawn points (see: this game), gameplay and narrative are intimately connected; character actions are justified, and power ups serve the story and the player. The result is that each accomplishment you make is both rewarding and intensely satisfying.

I testify to what others have said: the game looks beautiful, sounds beautiful, plays beautifully. Everything about it is stunning. But don't be fooled: it's beautiful *and* hard. If you aren't a skilled platformer now, play Ori and the Blind Forest. You will be.

I very, very rarely review games, so I'm doing this out of sheer respect and thankfulness for the developer, Moon Studios.

Ori is easily [b] one of the best games [/b] I have bought on a whim (in 8 years of Steam), and had I had any idea of that... well, it wouldn't have been on a whim. The art is probably what stands out the most, but that's only because the controls are so well implemented, they never really took me out of this immersive - and touching - story. Not for a second, honestly.

It was sufficiently challenging for me as a seasoned gamer, but I'm more than sure it shouldn't be frustrating for any casual gamer who doesn't possess a really, really short temper. In fact, [b]I cannot think of another game that made me care so little about dying[/b] and having to repeat the same difficult scenes. To the opposite: I was so excited by them (in no small part thanks to the amazing soundtrack and artwork that surely accompanied), that I sometimes died on purpose at the end of a tough part to try to play it again more perfectly. I feel like this is a really big deal and I hope you believe me.

I can honestly think of only one con: you cannot (as of yet at least) continue playing your save after you finish the game. I wish I had known this before, because I truly wanted to go back and finish it 100% - something I'm not at all used to - but I'm sure I'll play through it again. By the way, I makes me happy that the Ori has TEN different slots for you and your family/friends to start a game on. I don't understand why so many games lack that.

In short, I HIGHLY recommend playing Ori, and [b]I can see no contraindications[/b] to warn buyers of. Gameplay, art and soundtrack are truly remarkable, and the story is surprising and nothing short of beautiful. This is a game that stands out, and one to remember for a long, long time. Thank you and congratulations to the developers for making such a brilliant game, and selling it for such fair price.

Things Ori reminded me of, while playing: Studio Ghibli, Rayman, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, Guacamelee, Disney, The Lion King...

I'll finish by quoting another reviewer: "[i]Oh how I wish there were more games like this one, especially when they come out of nowhere like this one did.[/i]"

[b] One of the best things I've played. [/b]

I am playing this game in 2023. I probably bought it in 2018 and played without a controller. It wasn't fun so I stopped playing. I recently bought a $20 controller from Amazon and got back to the game and oh man, this is the best game I have played since a long time. I am 35 while writing this review and I hadn't enjoyed a game like this since about 2004.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a perfect platformer.
It looks great, the soundtrack is fantastic, storyline is quite interesting (and touching!) too.
The world design is absolutely incredible. And the fact that world changes after your actions is pretty cool too.
But if you think that those cutesy looks cover a basic platformer - you cannot be mistaken more.
This game is hard as hell. At some points I would even call it "torture platformer" because, well, it's a torture to get through those segments.
But when you actually do - it's incredibly satisfying. I'd say it's very close to Dark Souls level of satisfaction after you figure out those hard parts.

Using the controller to play works best, but keyboard works pretty well too.
Oh, and did I mentioned this game was made using Unity? Next time someone says Unity is crap, show him this game.

You can beat Ori in slightly more than 6h. I think 6h at the moment is best time in leaderboards. Took me 6h40m (and a lot of deaths) to beat it with 60% completion. So, it's not a very long game. That might be a bit of a downside for some 
But I'd say it definitely does worth those $20.

Other minor downside include a couple of smaller bugs (e.g. right trigger not working or 360-pad in some cases) that are known, do not harm the gameplay in a significant way and are being fixed.

More detailed look in the video:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rCFTGHrrW1A

I have been waiting for this game since E3 2014 and boy does it deliver. Absolutely breathtaking visuals, wonderful ambient soundtrack, and an emotional story that brought me to tears less than 5 minutes into the game. It's also a pretty challenging platformer with some light RPG elements, so there's plenty to like about it.

Do yourself a favor and buy this game. You won't regret it.

And incredibly well made platformer. Looks and feels amazing and has a fantastic soundtrack. It's not flawless, the combat system for example isn't very enjoyable, but thankfully it isn't a huge part of the experience. The strongest aspect of the game is definitly the movement system, especially the bash mechanic, which is something unique that I haven't seen in other games before.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of those games that reminds you why simple gameplay, when done right, still works. It’s a beautiful 2D platformer that focuses on movement, timing, and flow rather than overwhelming you with systems or clutter.

The progression feels natural. You unlock abilities as you play, and each one meaningfully changes how you move through the world. Backtracking never feels like a chore because new skills open up paths that previously felt impossible. The platforming itself is tight, responsive, and satisfying, especially once the movement really clicks.

What stood out most to me was how easy it is to just sit down, grab a controller, and play. No friction. No unnecessary complexity. You fail, you retry, you improve. The difficulty spikes are real, but they feel earned, and overcoming them is genuinely rewarding.

Add to that the art style and music, which do a lot of heavy lifting emotionally without needing excessive dialogue, and you end up with a game that feels focused and confident in what it wants to be.

Ori and the Blind Forest doesn’t try to reinvent the genre. It just executes it extremely well.

Full Price Recommendation.

This is the first game I've ever felt warranted a full, serious review from me, and for good reason. I don't know if anyone will ever see this glowing review in the thousands of other glowing reviews, but this game was so good that I felt like it was worth it just on the off chance that anyone might be convinced to buy this game. As a fan of metroidvania style games, this is one of my favorite games of all time.
Everything is executed masterfully. So well in fact, that I could write a semi-essay analyzing everything this game does right. And I will. 

Level Design- There are so many gameplay aspects that Ori and the Blind Forest succeeds in where others fail. The most important one is diverse level design. Where many "indie" platformers usually fall a bit flat is maintaining diversity of gameplay through their level design. After a while many games start to feel repettive and boring. Ori and the Blind Forest avoids this problem throughout the entire game. Never once while playing did I feel like I was trudging through a level that was boring just so I could get to the next big boss or dungeon. Every section of the map was unique, focusing on a particular gimmick or technique. What's more, many of the "themes" of each section served to teach the player how to use new abilities, meaning that long, wordy, and often confusing tutorials were never necesarry. Not a single part of the map felt unecessary or like "filler". You never spend to much time on one map section and it's theme before moving on to a different one, and this made the entire gameplay expirience unique and intresting.

Progression- Ori and the Blind Forest also does something that many other games ignore all together. A sense of world and character progression. Many games fail to give the player a tangible sense that what they're doing is changing the world or character for the better in any way, other than showing they've progressed to the "next level". In Ori and the Blind Forest, the major "dungeons", (the three elements that the player must restore), fundamentally change the entire map once they are beaten. I won't spoil it, but restoring each element allows easier and greater access to many parts of the map that were previously hard or impossible to get to, and leads to drastic asethtic changes as well. The player can return to previous sections and see these changes and access new areas, which really builds a sense of purpose and progession. In addition, the way new abilities are spaced out and slowly gained throughout the game really feels like the character is learning how to survive along with the player. 

Gameplay- Gameplay is where Ori and the Blind Forest really shines. The designers of this game have really quite ingeniously found so many different ways to expand upon the platformer expirience and incorporate their character abilities into their level design in new and intresting ways. All of the abilities the character gains serve a purpose and are simplistic and easy to pick up, yet open countless new ways that the player might move and interact with the world around him. Once you pick up an ability, you'll end up using it until the end of the game, even if some level sections focus more on one ability. No ability is unecesarry and given to the player specifically for one section only to be forgotten later; a probelm prevalent in other games. Each ability combines seamlessly with one another, and the player will often find him or herself executing rapid combinations of moves in succession without even conciously realizing it. The controls are so smooth and well-integrated with each other and the level design that the player begins to feel like his or her brain is being directly transported inside the body of the main character, and he or she is inside the game itself. 

Difficulty- Difficulty is the aspect of the game that is most criticized and probably the hardest to tackle, due to the diverse levels of skill and comfort in platforming. Many casual gamers or people who usually play different types of games often complain that the game is way too challenging, and report getting stuck on some sections and dying literally hundreds of times throughout the entire game. But Since I was already an avid platformer before I picked up the game, I found the initial playthrough challenging but not overly difficult. The main challenge for me was finding out what to do. This game is a true homage to the Metroidvania era, and has minimal guidance or direction. The game is as much of a puzzle game as it is a platformer, and many sections will require a lot of creative thinking to get through. In my opinion, the puzzles are well designed and rewarding, but if puzzles are not your cup of tea and you want to get straight into the jumping, there are extensive tutorials on youtube, so it shouldn't be much of an issue. The more complicated issue is the difficulting of the actual platforming. There's no way to "adjust" the difficulty of the actual jumps, and more inexpirienced players may have harder times trying to execute manuvers. Thankfully, there are many things the game designers subtly incoporated to make the game easier. First of all, Ori and the Blind Forest uses a very liberal save system that gives the player a high degree of flexibility regarding where and how many times the player can save. A good and concious managment of where you chose to save can drastically improve your gameplay expirience, and prevent the player from repeating difficult parts over and over again. Secondly, there are powerups hidden throughout the map that allow the player to access an upgrade tree or increase the player's max life or save capacity. Many of these powerups will be initially unreachable but can later be accessed once the player gains new abilities are returns to previous sections. Spending a bit of time returning to and thouroughly exploring old sections to collect all these powerups can make the game significantly easier. For the rare hardcore gamer who thinks the game is too easy, the game can be made a lot more difficult by simply not collecting these powerups, or setting challenges for yourself like no-damage runs.

Plot- The plot at its core is a very simplistic and classic concept. It's not anything too mind-blowing or special, but it works well with the story, setting, and design of the game. The main focus of the game is the gameplay, but the story IS there and it's executed well. The cutscenes are also very well done, meaning that what little story is there is emotionally resinant and heartwarming.

Animation, Art, Worldbuilding- These are the parts of the game that are most commonly cited as the "main thing" Ori and the Blind Forest has got going for it, and while I think that is cutting the other amazingly well done aspects of the game short, I can definitely see where people are coming from when they say this. The Art is absolutely stunning, and everything, from the background, the enemies, the plants, to the character itself is animated masterfully. Everything comes together to create a quintessential fantasy aesthetic that is both familiar and at the same time completely unique. The entire world feels alive, and I mean it in every sense of the word. The way everything is drawn and moves is smooth and natural, and I have no doubt there are many times that I was wishing that I could leave the far uglier world of reality behind and be transported into the game. The designers left in so many tiny details to ensure that the world never felt like it was just "part of a video game". It felt like the player only got to see a rare glimpse of a far larger universe, and that there are countless other stories in its world that simply remain untold.

In conclusion, Ori and the Blind Forest is a stunning example of what can be achieved when a development team puts their heart and passion into their work; I can not recommend this game any more than I already have.

Ori 1 is a good platformer game which focus more on jumping and bashing more than boss fights.  Overall it's a pleasant experience and quite relaxing to play.  Note that the skill bash allows a few seconds to adjust its direction.  I didn't realise that in the 1st run and suffered many unnecessary deaths. 

Achievement difficulty overall is not too bad.  Three areas in the game will be locked when completed, which may cause some issues for collection achievements.  No death, no skill and speed run achievements can be completed in the same run.  I did it on the 3rd run with less than 2 hours, with the help of the duplicate saves function in game. 

I played 80% of the time on steam deck and 20% of the time on PC.  The switching between deck and PC is hassle-free.  However, there seems to be some glitches in achievements when playing on deck.  I got two achievements (50% and 100% map stones) unlocked in early part of the 1st run when the criteria is not met.  There is also a noticeable difference between the 60 fps on deck and 120 fps on PC.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a game everyone should experience at least once, I will never forget Ori and Naru adventure and I hope to play this game with my kids in the future...

Absolutely loved this game -- parts of it were incredibly difficult, and I died more times than I care to remember, but the story and the gameplay were great.  There were a few glitches, like the game crashing (maybe 5 times in 25 hours of gameplay, my hours played is inflated due to some idling), but in general very smooth. 10/10 Amazing.

Pros:
-Gorgeous graphics
-Fantastic, challenging gameplay
-Beautiful soundtrack

Cons:
-Can't re-enter certain areas to pick up missed things
-Framerate froze a couple times during the big cutscenes
-May be too difficult for some

Honestly, I've read a lot of the negative reviews here on Steam, and most of them complain that the game is too difficult, and in fact, it's just poorly designed and they had to make it so that you can save anywhere to make up for the poor level design.

THAT IS RIDICULOUS. 

Yes, the game does have some difficult platforming challenges... But this is intentional, and the save system complements this. You respawn in a fraction of a second and you don't get that helpless feeling of being dead and having to wait for it to load again, like in a lot of games.

Super Meat Boy is another extremely challenging game that does this well: the levels are small but the challenge is huge, but you die and respawn so quick that you're never sitting around waiting.

And just like Super Meat Boy, when you finally do get through a really tough section it feels so rewarding. 

I'd much rather die repeatedly in one spot for 3 minutes then have an entire game that doesn't challenge me.

The game only took 10 hours to beat, which is surprising because it felt like much more. It's a big world and the complexity builds nicely throughout the game. But I know for sure this is a game I will play over again and again.

[b]I’ll be honest, I played the last 2D game was Sonic the Hedgehog, after playing Crysis I was never a 2D platform gamer. The genre never really pulled me in, and I always gravitated towards other types of games. But then I stumbled upon Ori and the Blind Forest, and let me tell you… this game changed everything.
From the moment I started playing, I was completely mesmerized. The visuals, the music, the atmosphere—it all blended together to create something truly magical. I came in as a skeptic, and I left as a huge fan.[/b]

[h1]A Visual and Artistic Masterpiece[/h1]
[b]I don’t think words can do justice to how stunning this game looks. Every frame feels like a living painting, with breathtaking environments that are rich in color and depth. The way light filters through the trees, the movement of Ori, and the sheer attention to detail in every level, it’s a feast for the eyes.
Even if you’ve never played a 2D platformer before, the art alone will keep you invested. Whether you’re exploring the lush greenery of the Sunken Glades or escaping a raging flood, every moment is visually unforgettable.[/b]

The orchestral pieces tug at your heartstrings, and the way the music swells during emotional moments is nothing short of perfection. I found myself just pausing at times, letting the music wash over me. It’s that powerful.[/b]

This is the kind of game that makes you reflect, not just on the story itself, but on themes of sacrifice, belonging, and the beauty of life. And when a game can do that? That’s something truly special.[/b]

With a seemingly never-ending flock of "retro" platformers hitting the Steam store these days, [i]Ori and the Blind Forest[/i] takes the opposite route: a story-driven adventure with stunning visuals, a bewitching atmosphere and some pretty mad feels.

The first thing that will captivate you is the sheer beauty of the game. The art, the characters and their animations, the lighting and the splendid instrumental music score will instantaneously create a deep feeling of immersion. The storytelling, most of which occurs in-game, will also be supported by small doses of narration and beautiful cutscenes, just enough to give you a sense of purpose and accomplishment.

The gameplay is everything you could possibly wish for: tight and responsive, with top-notch level design and an increasing number of mechanisms to master as you progress, in pure Metroidvania fashion. The overall difficulty achieves a fine balance, making [i]Ori[/i] both accessible to players who just want to enjoy the story and atmosphere, and challenging enough at times to keep veteran players on their toes. Exploration is rewarded with power-ups that give you more leeway to fill the simple-yet-efficient skill tree, which nicely complements the other abilities that you unlock as you advance through the game.

A casual playthrough will last you a good 10 hours, and that alone would be well worth themoney. But [i]Ori[/i] also nudges the more hardcore players into giving it another go with an online speed run leaderboard and some pretty tight achievements like completing the game without dying. All in all, a very fair amount of content for its price tag with refined quality on top of that. The standard for an up-to-date adventure platformer and a definite recommendation for me.

Ori and the Blind Forest is an action platformer with a strong emphasis on movement and platforming. While the beautiful graphics and amazing soundtrack seem relaxing at first the game itself actually isn’t, therefore be aware that it becomes quite challenging pretty fast.

I bought the game right after release back in 2015, when I was quite an impatient gamer and easily frustrated. Tried playing it, didn’t get very far. Tried again some three years later after buying a gamepad, got a bit further, but again quit at quite an early stage. I assumed it just wasn’t for me until I got back to it this year when a friend played it for the first time, and after learning that the Definitive Edition had an easy mode and fast travel. I played through the Definitive Edition and suddenly found that it was actually manageable. Also I started loving the movement in the game - so fast, dynamic and beautiful that I found it hard to play something else because everything felt so slow. And so I decided to play the original game again, mainly because I had just a handful of achievements and wanted to improve my statistics.

Well, it started to get addictive. In just about two weeks I played through the game several times, got every achievement, even the harder ones that I didn’t do in DE, and I can honestly say I love the game and I’ve completely grown into it. For me it isn’t really difficult anymore, which is amazing looking at how I started off. Also, despite having played through the whole game about four or five times in a row for the last few days, it doesn’t start to get boring yet. So I think it comes as no surprise that I recommend the game very much. For the amazing visuals, the soundtrack, the fluid and fun movement mechanics. 
The story is okay, it’s nothing innovative or exceptional, but it’s nice and I don’t mind the lack of depth at all because this is one of the games that I mainly play for the gameplay and not the story. 
I personally would recommend playing with a controller.

I really start to appreciate the differences the original has compared to DE. The extra areas in the Definitive Edition are a nice addition, yet I didn’t actually miss them in my runs in the original game. I also didn’t miss difficulty settings any more. The main difference is the checkpoints during the escape sequences I think, and yes, it does get frustrating to restart at the beginning of the sequence just because of one little mistake or wrong timing. But all in all the sequences aren’t long and they can be learned - and eventually completing them in one go feels so much more dynamic and satisfying. Also, I didn’t miss fast travel at all. Only thing that can be annoying is that you cannot enter certain areas again after you’ve completed them, whereas in DE you can. In the original game I had some performance issues from time to time but not that often and nothing problematic.

There is just one thing that I found myself thinking during most of the recent playthroughs but I’m not actually sure whether it’s really bothering me: There are some platforming elements that I found interesting but that were used only in their specific areas so you don’t encounter them again after just a few times that you have to use them. While it makes sense in most cases, it felt a bit weird to me in others.

Another thing I want to address as the games are often compared is the differences to Hollow Knight. The game’s focus is different. Ori is much more about platforming than combat, and it isn’t as large as Hollow Knight, the playtime is much shorter. So if you’re coming from Hollow Knight, just don’t expect too much in those areas. You’re probably going to enjoy the game a lot more if you don’t compare those two, and it wouldn’t do it justice as Ori is still quite a different and beautiful experience on its own.

Ori and the Blind Forest feels like Nintendo’s second coming.

Despite having no connection to the revered developer you can see Nintendo’s fingerprints everywhere in Ori, in a way that’s deeper than rudimentary inspiration or recreation. It’s a design philosophy, one which wraps around Ori and grants it a feeling of immense knowledge and cohesion. This may be Moon Studio’s first release, but it brings with it the passion and insight present in so many of the most beloved games ever released while simultaneously transcending them, feeling like the next step forward rather than a mere imitation.

Ori’s mechanical building blocks exist in a space that’s been exhaustively tapped and refined over the years (especially in the modern indie game industry), yet here take on a newfound innovation. It isn’t about “what” Ori is doing, so much as “how” is is executing it. There are countless precision and Metroid-like platformers now superficially working off almost the exact same routine as Ori, but what elevates Ori above them is its cohesion and forward thinking. It isn’t a collection of easily marketed parts assembled into a bizarre collage of styles and eras, but an astoundingly refined and unified vision that shares the same DNA as many of its peers but doesn’t allow that to define it.

The most impressive aspect of Ori is in how everything is working together toward the same goal. Level designs combine with a steady progression to create a sense of constant forward momentum; the presentation conjoins with Ori’s movements to feel alive and organic; ideas expand and elaborate on themselves as the difficulty scales to match, breaking at just the right moments to never hinder the pacing.

The level of skill with which Ori executes itself is remarkably precise and considered, even more so given its immense confidence which constantly reaffirms Moon Studios knows exactly what they’re doing. It’s not arrogant; it’s what allows Ori to so successfully advance beyond what has already been done.

One of the most surprising aspects of Ori to me is how despite utilizing many of Metroid’s (and maybe to an even bigger extent Zelda’s) progression systems, backtracking is almost nonexistent. You might pass through a repeated area here and there (or if you want to head back and pick up some stuff you missed), but there is almost always a reason for it which drastically alters how you now travel from A to B. Ori makes revisiting old areas engaging because it almost never feels like the same area anymore. Your abilities grow so quickly and steadily that by the time you return to a familiar spot you are now traversing it in a totally different way. This eliminated one of my biggest grievances with this style of game, in that so often they seem to start and stop as you travel between one area to the next, requiring you to retread old ground almost exactly as you already did once before. That never happens in Ori, which meant I was constantly engaged in what I was doing and how.

Where Ori had the biggest chance to fall apart was its difficulty, which is shockingly steep from the start and only goes up the further you progress. This is offset by how much can be visually understood about Ori’s level designs and how your character moves within them. Everything in Ori is in constant motion and with a great deal of discernible weight, which allows you to immediately know how far you’ll go with a jump, what’s in your path, and how you need to move past it. This certainly doesn’t make Ori anything approaching easy, but it does make it intuitive and approachable. It also makes it extremely fun just to move around and navigate the world, because it feels like you’re actually there interacting with it, feeling it move, discovering its secrets, and Moon has wisely left just enough room for human error that movement always feels organic and dynamic.

It’s also hard to miss how breathtaking the world you’re traveling through is, though it’s even harder to explain that through words alone. Suffice it to say that whatever you thinking Ori looks like or how impressive it seems from the outside, it’s nothing like experiencing it first hand and being a part of it. Ori is a technical marvel, sure, through its multilayered presentation, the astounding framing (with just subtle enough an angle to give it depth), and how impossibly smoothly Ori animates in collaboration with it. What blew me away though is how it never stops topping itself, and how much it is able to hold back for its most awe-inspiring moments while still being staggeringly pretty. It manages the difficult balance between wow-ing the player and not overwhelming them, and by the end even calling it the most gorgeous game I’ve ever played seemed an understatement.

There are a lot of easy things to praise Ori and the Blind Forest for, but it really is in how it comes together that makes it such a rich and enjoyable experience. It’s the feeling I get when I play things like Super Mario 3 or Super Metroid, which despite their age still present some of the best examples of concise, cohesive design which is missing from so many games. Ori understands this on a very deep level, and through that has created something  magnificent. It very well might be something that you can only understand through playing it yourself, but trust me when I say that’s something you want to do.

    Story: plot was simple. It was just a story about a little animal influenced enemies with his kindness. It was very simple and enough for a platformer game which lasts about 10 hours in length. Other creatures except Ori didn’t show strong and obvious personalities. But it seemed they were designed to be creatures which didn’t know how to express their feeling so it was fair. I believe most players might be very touched by the big bird’s sacrifice for Ori.

Although the difficulty is high to most people, there are some talented people post some videos like “speedrun” “zero death”...etc. I watched those video and the operation was too amazing to do. At least I couldn’t do it at all.


     Conclusion: flawless graphics, surprising soundtrack, simple but touching story, high difficulty with friendly save mode, if you love platformer games, Ori and The Blind Forest will never let you down. Sadly, Ori and the Blind Forest does not live up to the hype. It is a good game which could be an amazing one if not for a plethora of flaws.

The biggest and most egregious flaw is that it seems to prioritise aesthetics over gameplay. It looks fantastic, but too often the foreground obscures part of the level, which is totally unacceptable for a 2D platformer. Even when the foreground doesn't obscure the level, it's not always clear what is in the foreground, what is in the background, and what is in the level itself. Furthermore, there isn't enough colour contrast; everything is so glowy that it becomes very difficult to pick out things like enemy projectiles, which can be tiny. Enemies themselves often blend in with the level too.

Another flaw is in the gameplay itself, which far too often comes down to trial and error. I may not be the best at platformers, but I'm not stupid. In other games I can appreciate how the levels guide me towards the correct solution without giving it away, but Ori lacks that guidance almost entirely, and I had to resort to looking up guides many times.

That trial-and-error gameplay is most evident in the game's four escape sequences, which I will bring up as a flaw in their own right, because they have another major issue: they represent an enormous difficulty spike over the rest of the game. This is particularly true in the Ginso Tree escape, which took me well over 50 attempts and made me give up playing altogether until a friend convinced me to keep trying. In the rest of the game, you can save almost anywhere, but in the escape sequences there is no saving and no checkpoints whatsoever, so you have to complete them in one go. That means dying repeatedly just to [I]see[/I] the next mechanic, let alone survive it. There's no advantage to completing the early part of the escape quickly, though, since whatever is chasing you (water, for example) is on an "elastic band" and will simply catch up with you. The escapes involve extensive use of the Bash skill to propel yourself off an enemy projectile, sometimes more than once in succession, which can be very frustrating when those projectiles don't appear in the right places or at the right times. One mistake is usually all it takes to die and go right back to the start.

(Side note: the irony in dying to a flood of clean water just after teaching Ori to breathe in clean water was not lost on me.)

Combat is dull and usually devolves to mashing the attack button as quickly as possible, since Bash doesn't do as much damage as the Spirit Flame and the other attacks are too situational. The UI is dumb - I don't need to be reminded that Energy can be used to save the game when I'm on the final level and I've saved 100 times already - and often gets in the way. Some of the controller bindings are questionable - I personally wouldn't have mapped two different functions to the right trigger, for example, when other buttons are completely unused. Having to move the analog stick to perform Stomps and Charges (but only when attached to a wall; there's a different button for performing them on the ground) is unnecessarily fiddly when the analog stick is already used for movement. There is no option to rebind the buttons, either. Cutscenes aren't skippable. You can't go back and gather collectibles after finishing the game - it even deletes your backup saves. The game crashed on me once when I opened the Steam Overlay.

I suppose I should also talk about the story. I could never escape the feeling that it was [I]trying[/I] to move me, rather than letting it happen naturally. The same goes for the music. As a result, I didn't feel any particularly strong emotions throughout the course of the game. The narration is rather too vague for my liking.

And you know something else I'm disappointed with? I have owned this game since before the Definitive Edition came out, but there is no discount for upgrading. Yes, I was given a voucher, but it has long since expired, and I wanted to decide whether to give Microsoft more of my money in my own time, not theirs. Compare and contrast the Special Edition of Skyrim, which I got completely free by virtue of owning the original game and its expansions.

There are lots of good things about Ori, which you can read in other reviews. I don't disagree with them - it is an enjoyable platformer at its core - but I don't feel the need to repeat them, either. For me, the bad outweighs the good. Not recommended.

[h1]A stunningly beautiful metroidvania platformer that is rock hard.[/h1]

The aesthetics are some of the best, if not the best, I've ever seen in any video game. Every background and foreground object is hand painted to awe-inspiring effect. This combined with the [url=http://majornelson.com/2015/03/11/ori-blind-forest-original-soundtrack/]incredible soundtrack from Gareth Coker[/url] adds up to be one of the most stunning displays I've had the pleasure of enjoying. On top of the amazing visuals and soundtrack, we have a heart-wrenching story to go with all this that will definitely leave at least some (me) in tears throughout.

Nestled within all this beauty is an exquisitely executed metroidvania platformer. Ori boasts fluid controls while still being extremely tight. It’s as if Moon Studios took the best aspects of Rayman Legends and Super Meat Boy’s controls with the result being a perfect marriage of the two vastly different titles. The progression of skills is steady and follows a logical succession. At first you’re barely able to jump over the smallest log, but by the end you’ll be nimble like the adorable little forest sprite that you are.

Above all else, this game is HARD. Maybe not as hard as some of the most infuriating levels of Super Meat Boy, but the inspiration definitely shows; be sure to save often because the last thing you want is to die unexpectedly and have to go through that hell again. Then again, maybe that is exactly what you want. In a market where it’s increasingly taboo to actually kill the player in a single player game, Ori has no qualms with killing you over, and over, and over again. That said, the deaths are never cheap or feel like the result of poor level design or other shenanigans; it’s abundantly clear that if you die, it’s your own fault.
I want everyone to play this game and love it as much as I do. I look forward to getting as many of the achievements that I can, no matter how difficult some of them seem to be.

To Moon Studios, thank you for delivering such an incredible experience. This is why I love video games. I can’t really express just how much I’ve fallen in love with Ori, Sein, Naru, Koru, and all the other characters in this masterpiece.

The game is quite fun as a platformer, brought a lot of challenge to the users, and gives me the sense of accomplishment whenever I squeeze through different challenges and difficult terrain and paths. I can see the development team put a lot of efforts in the story, graphics, music and gameplay. It was really fun to play, and I got addicted to it for days before I finished the whole game.
However, the control is painful, especially for keyboard players, as my hand and fingers almost got a cramp pressing the damn glide button, I think the control is actually quite bad for a well polished game like this, sometimes you have to press it again and again in a short period of time, only to dodge the spikes and obstacles, and sometimes you have to hold as long as it can just to glide through the stream of air. It could be much better if using a controller to play this game. But it isn't so friendly to keyboard players, as the shift button is really not the best position to either hold it for a long time or pressing it repeatedly, your hands would really get screwed. I guess swapping the button assignments of bashing and gliding/climbing would be much better.
On the other hand, the game is pretty straight forward, IMO it lacks variety compared to Castlevania and Bloodstained. The monsters are pretty much the same and they don't really stand an important role in the way of your journey, just to let you bash through them to find new paths, or restoring energy or health. For me the monsters set up in the game is also very important in a platformer game, however I think this game lacks it. The game will get a bit more repetitive as it goes through the story especially mid to late game, but it is still fun as it is quite challenging. It just lacks replayability.
All in all, this game is great in many ways but some short comings are just really painful and agonising. Sometimes really make me feel like giving it up. 
Anyone who hasn't played this wonderful game should try it as soon as you can, you will fall in love straight away.

At first, I thought Ori and the Blind Forest was just going to be a beautiful game with basic gameplay. Not only does it play really well, but it also blew me away with its graphics, music and its touching story even though I knew what the game looked like before I played it. But it's only when you start playing (with a controller or keyboard/mouse, both work well) that you get it. Just watching the game is not enough ; you have to play it to fully understand what the game really wants you to feel.

It's not an easy game, but it's not so hard that it makes you wanna punch your screen or anything. I've read some complaints about the game having too much "die & retry" in it. I disagree, as there are only 2, maybe 3 scenes in the game that can be considered that. The game always stays fair though, and it's just hard enough to make you feel like you're never really safe, even though you already picked every single health bonus you can get.

And those bonus can be really fun to look for. As a metroid-vania, you'll have to come back to some parts of the world using shortcuts you just created with your new powers. There's no teleportation here, everything is connected, yet it never feels like a pain to go back anywhere. Maybe it's thanks to the amazing graphics and music, but travelling back to a place you've already been to is always a pleasure. But it won't just be running, as enemies are always present in the game and will respawn.

Combat is pretty simple and easy ; press a button and a homing attack will deal damage to an enemy. You still have to dodge though, as Ori is very fragile, especially early in the game when getting killed in one or two hits is not rare. It gets easier though as you gain points by killing enemies and finding sometimes well hidden orbs to make your little guy stronger or to show things on the map. You can create a save point yourself, and you should since the default save points are rare. It has a cooldown and requires energy though, but those can be reduced if you spend your points in the right place.

And saving is really important, since you'll die a lot. Not necessarily because of enemies, but because of the platforming element of the game. Don't get me wrong; the game controls perfectly and some moves are just amazing both to look at and to do. Some jumps are not easy, even though it never gets as crazy as, let's say, Super Meat Boy, but none of them feels unfair. Sometimes you'll get to a place and wonder how you're supposed to make a jump that seems impossible to do, but in the end you just do it naturally. I won't spoil the moves you get later in the game, but I'll just say that I've never liked the "Y" button on my controller that much before.

In short, this game is a masterpiece. If I had to find something wrong with the game, I'd say the game is a bit short (I read 10+ hours, I finished the game in less than 7 hours, taking my time and exploring a lot). For 20 eurodollars (I'd say the same for 40 though), this is a game I highly encourage you to buy. And buy the soundtrack too, even though it isn't the same without the rest of the game, it's still amazing.

I've owned this game for a few weeks already, and I still haven't come to terms with its abject, unadulterated beauty. I could talk about the controls or the level design, which are normally the most important points for me for any platformer... If I did that, I would be comparing it favorably to the best platformers I've ever played. But in spite of the game's excellence in those areas, it is its visual and musical supremacy that sticks in my mind.

Friends of mine, even friends who don't normally like platformers, beg me to stream this game for them, equating it to "audiovisual crack". Occasionally—even after my third full playthrough—I find myself stopping, overwhelmed for a few moments by what I'm seeing. It has set a new visual standard for me, one which every other game I've played to date falls well short of achieving.

As for the music... In-game, it is sublime and nearly seamless. It isn't that it sets the mood of the game, nor vice versa; the soundtrack and the rest of the game simply... complete each other. Perfectly. To the note. And, listening to bits of the soundtrack outside the focusing influence of the game itself, I find myself moved in ways I have [b]never[/b] been moved by music before.

I am normally loquacious and pride myself on my vocabulary, but words completely fail me when I try to describe how this game looks and sounds and feels. Very few games have had this kind of impact on me. This is the sort of release that comes once per decade, or less.

Based on classic gameplay but improved, wonderful art, few drops of story in the right moments with a high concentration of feelings and an amusing soundtrack.

[h1][i]INTRO. What is Ori And The Blind Forest about?[/i][/h1]
I don't want to spoil anything because, as I've already mentioned, there are few short moments of story and the introduction is one of the most important.
However I can say that you play as Ori, a newborn creature lost inside a forest and guided by Sein, a creature of light that knows the story of all the places. The forest used to be alive but now and a pleasant place to live but now it's dark and dying and you must recover the light of three elements to restore the forest and heal the Great Spirit Tree. Sounds uninteresting, I know, but everything I didn't say is worth every second. And I didn't say a lot. I can say that it can get very touching and involving since the introduction and through the whole game.

[h1][i]GRAPHIC. Engine And Artistic aspects.[/i][/h1]
Who would have thought that Ori was developed with Unity? Yes, it was done with Unity and it's marvelous, polished and well coded. And all landscapes and characters are simply marvelous as well, with beautiful drawn locations and colorful enemies it's just a pleasure to play and watch.

[h1][i]SOUNDTRACK. Themes and Accompaniments.[/i][/h1]
One of the strongest parts of the game. All tracks are just amazing symphonic movements, with occasional choirs and have that "something" that give you the perfect feeling and mood for the situation, being exploration, a boss stage or an escape. I still occasionally listen to it.

[h1][i]GAMEPLAY. How does it work?[/i][/h1]
Ori and The Blind Forest is basically a 2d platform. For each beaten enemy you gain experience to obtain specific abilities ranging from passive skills such as increased amount of energy/life/xp per pickup to useful skills as double jumps.
An important thing I've underestimated is the ability to save at any point you wish. You spend a couple of energy balls but it's worth the effort. Because the other thing I've underestimated is the game's difficulty! It's not impossible, but you must be considerate in your sessions because enemies can be more dangerous the more you proceed (obviously) and most importantly there are many environmental threats and the combination of both represent a big difficulty if you underestimate them.

I don't see any trouble or mistake in this game... Really...

5 years late, but let me start off buy calling it "masterpiece". I didn't play the DE version, though I am made aware of certain changes and addition to the game which I sorta fell unnecessary. So let me point out a few key strengths (an INTENDED flaws) of this game.

[u]1. GAME MECHANICS[/u]
The core mechanics is action platformer, with majority of the maneuver focusing on movements rather than combat. I love the fact that it doesn't have the fine precision of traditional platformers where the latter are very unforgiving. Because of that, Ori brings a great sense of accomplishment when you achieve certain level of mastery for maneuvering around the map. Ori also introduces a mechanic called Bash which I think is one of the smartest core mechanics in recent times. One of the criticism I heard was about its lack of combat. Personally I think it was intended design and find it without strong emphasis on combat. Lastly would be the difficulty. I find the lack of difficulty settings as a bold design choice. It makes the game to be played as the developers intended and I applaud it.

[u]2. MUSIC SCORE[/u]
Music score is perfect, nothing more I can add but to give my highest compliment. It is not just memorable, but certain tracks were incredibly designed to be modular so it can fit the action, stage and transition perfectly.

[u]3. LEVEL DESIGN[/u]
The level design is incredibly well done. Each challenge and obstacle in the map is well position. It is always done in the manner where it doesn't "punish" the player but a "challenge" instead. One great example is health and energy resources are placed at spots where the developers knew you will have a tough time. Some other subtlety would be the music score designed to encourage the players to brave through the challenges. Each chapter presents you new location with fresh challenges and requires you to combine different skills and maneuvers to overcome it, thus eliminate the repetitiveness like other platformers do.

[u]4. VISUAL AESTHETICS[/u]
The game has incredible palettes. Despite different level requires different palette to convey the mood and atmosphere, there isn't a single moment where I feel it is monotonous. The higher saturation artstyle and the crisp graphics give a new breath to the stall platforming genre. This also addresses a beef I had with many platformers, where they exploit sense of nostalgia by using 8-bit and 16-bit art style. I mean for Christ's sake we are living in the 21st century. Can't we make fun games but also utilizing modern graphic tools? Sadly they don't have any published artbooks which I would love to own.
